title: The White Water
passages:
They did not stop at the hut. Tomas pulled a skiff from beneath the landing and Ákos stepped in, the thread clenched in his fist. It warmed against his palm, then hotter, as if it knew the direction before he did. Tomas took the oars and they pushed off into the current.

The river narrowed past the first bend and the water began to climb against itself. Ákos watched the banks slip by, the thread a live coal in his closed hand. At the second bend the river threw up white water, a standing wave of churn and spray. On the far gravel bar, Kornél's boat lay on its side, the oars missing.

“There,” Ákos said.

Tomas shook his head. “That water will take the skiff.”

“It already took Kornél.” Ákos stood and braced himself. “Hold us off the stone. I’m going over.”

Tomas cursed but shipped the oars and held the skiff against the current while Ákos stepped onto the wetted rock. The thread burned now, a wire pulled tight. He crossed the swiftest channel waist-deep, the cold water shocking against his legs, and hauled himself onto the far bank. Kornél sat beneath a willow’s overhang, shirtless, staring at the rapids as if they had answered him.

Ákos held out his hand. “The thread. Ruzsa sent it.”

Kornél looked at it, then at Ákos, and reached out with his right hand. The moment the coil touched his skin the heat left Ákos’s palm and sank into Kornél’s. The thread went dark and cold, unspooling a single length of black thread into Kornél’s fingers. Kornél closed his fist around it and said, “Elise.” The water noise seemed to drop away.

Kornél’s fist tightened around the cold coil, the black thread humming against his palm as the roar of the water fell silent, as if the river itself were holding its breath. A flash of Elise’s face flickered in his mind, bright and then gone, leaving a hollow ache where her memory had been. He stared at the dark thread, feeling the weight of a debt that was no longer just a name but a promise that demanded something of him.  
While Sára slept, the ledger’s ink moved of its own accord, spelling a new line in her cramped hand: ‘Kornél owes the Toll House a fragment of his past.’ The weight of Ákos’s notebook shifted, the page swelling as if a hidden ledger inside were counting the cost; Maren’s warning rang in his ears, that every gift carries a price, and the price now glowed on the page, waiting for a memory to be given.  
Kornél rose, the cold thread pulling at his sleeve like a rope, and met Ákos’s steady gaze. He knew the river would not wait, and the white water behind him threatened to swallow the skiff and any lingering doubt. With a breath that tasted of iron, he turned toward the gravel bar, ready to walk the distance back to the Toll House, where the ledger might record his sacrifice before the next bell rang.

Kornél stepped into the current. The water bit at his thighs and the thread went slack, then heavy, pulling toward the white water as if it wanted to be taken. He stopped at the deepest channel and uncurled his fingers. “I give you the sound of her voice,” he said to the river. “The way she called my name the night the boat went down. Take it.”

The black coil in his palm shuddered. A grey wisp left his wrist and ran into the dark fiber. Kornél flinched, not from pain but from the sudden absence. He tried to call *Elise* and heard nothing. The thread turned warm, then bright, the black length unwinding into pale yarn that slid into the water and vanished.

“It’s gone,” Kornél said.

Ákos shouted from the bank, “Then come back.”

The current had pushed them downstream. Tomas held the skiff nose into the rapids, oars ready, while Kornél crossed back, waist-deep and shaking, the warm thread now a thin cord around his wrist that did not burn. Tomas caught his arm and hauled him into the skiff. They rowed hard against the standing wave until the gravel bar fell behind them and the first bend swallowed the roar.

Tomas beached the skiff on their side and stepped out onto the mud. Ákos pulled the cord from Kornél’s wrist and looked at it. “It’s only string now.”

Kornél nodded, touching his empty palm. “Elise is written. I paid what the thread asked.”

Ákos folded the cord into his pocket. “Then we walk to the Toll House. Sára’s ledger is waiting.”

Then we walk to the Toll House. Sára's ledger is waiting, its pages still warm from the night's work. A new entry catches the eye: 'Kornél owes the Toll House a fragment of his past.' Beside it, the spent cord from Kornél's wrist—already claimed as ordinary string by Ákos—lies humming, a faint vibration that seems to rise from the paper itself.

The sound is subtle, almost like a string being plucked, but it catches everyone's attention. The cord, which Ákos had insisted was now just ordinary string, responds to the ledger's presence. Sára watches, her breath shallow, as the hum grows slightly stronger when the cord is positioned nearer to the ink-stained page.

Outside the Toll House, the morning light catches Ákos's face as he shifts the cord in his pocket. Tomas stands ready, one hand on the skiff rope, the other gripping his silence. Kornél stares at the river below, the white water still roaring in his memory though his mind no longer holds Elise's voice.

Kornél steps forward, hand outstretched toward the ledger. The humming cord gives him pause. He looks from the vibrating string to Sára's face, searching for guidance.

Sára lifts her gaze from the ledger. Her eyes hold years of unspoken judgment. She tilts her head slightly—a lifetime of gestures replacing words. She had not spoken in years, yet her expression is clear: the debt is recorded, the cord is present, and the toll must be claimed or released.

Ákos shifts in his pocket. "She decides," he says, though Sára has made no sound. "The ledger speaks for her."

Kornél nods and places the cord beside the entry. The humming stops. The ledger's ink settles, the new line becoming still. Sára's hand, usually the one that writes, now hovers over the words she wrote in sleep. She has the power to claim the toll, to take her piece, or to let the matter rest. The morning light catches the edges of the ledger page, and for a moment, the weight of what has been done—and what could still be undone— hangs in the air between them.

Sára picked the cord up between two fingers. It was warm, and somewhere inside it a woman laughed — short, surprised, cut off. Kornél's head came up. He had heard nothing; she could see that from his face. The sound was hers alone, held in the Toll House's keeping.

She laid the cord on the open page and reached for the pen. Ákos started forward. "You don't write when you're awake," he said. Sára looked at him, then at the ledger, and wrote beneath the entry in a hand that was unmistakably her own: *Released.* The ink paled as it dried, going gray, then nothing. The hum stopped. Kornél let out a long breath and sat down on the bench as though his legs had been cut from under him.

She tried to add the date under it, as she did every morning. Her fingers would not close. She turned the hand over, pressed the thumb into the palm, waited. Nothing came back. The pen rolled out of her grip and clicked against the table.

Ákos picked it up and held it out. "Sára." She shook her head once and pushed the ledger toward him, open, the next page blank beneath her dead hand. The boy looked down at the pen, then at the empty lines, and understood what she was asking before she had to ask it.

Outside, the river went on. Kornél sat with his hands loose in his lap, free and empty, and Tomas watched the water and said nothing at all.
